metadata.file_name: Enrolment in the first stage of early childhood education and students  academic performance  a cross-country analysis.pdf
metadata.title: Enrolment in the first stage of early childhood education and students’ academic performance: a cros

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2011 and PIRLS 2016 fourth-grade reading data for 39 overlapping countries, and it explicitly states that PIRLS-recommended practices were applied to obtain representative results. Specifically, it reports using student weights, jackknife repeated replication (JRR) replicate weights, and five plausible values for the reading outcome. The analytic sample is restricted to the 39 countries listed in the paper and to students with the relevant background/home questionnaire information for FSECE attendance and the covariates used in the OLS/2SLS specifications. The manuscript does not name the exact PIRLS weight variable codes, but the use of PIRLS weights and JRR indicates complex survey design handling consistent with IEA guidance.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports the use of PIRLS student weights, jackknife repeated replication weights, and five plausible values, but it does not describe a specific missing-data strategy for questionnaire covariates or the FSECE indicator. This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect both the first-stage instrument relevance and the second-stage reading-score estimates in an instrumental-variables framework. Given the large PIRLS sample and multiple covariates, the absence of an explicit rule (e.g., complete-case vs. imputation) limits reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PIRLS 2011 and PIRLS 2016 fourth-grade reading data and restricts the analysis to the 39 countries common to both cycles (explicitly listed in the Notes). The dependent variable is students’ standardized reading scores (mean 0, SD 1) and the key treatment is a home-questionnaire indicator for whether the child attended an early childhood educational programme/centre for children under age 3 (FSECE, ISCED 0 first stage). The OLS and 2SLS models include student background characteristics (sex, age, reading time at home), family characteristics (father’s and mother’s education, father’s occupation, number of books at home), and the PIRLS cycle indicator; the 2SLS instrument is mother’s occupation measured when students are in fourth grade. The paper does not provide a separate explicit rule for excluding cases with missing covariates beyond the PIRLS-recommended practices, so the filtering is best described as using the available PIRLS microdata for the specified countries and variables required by the model.

main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS (Table 1): FSECE coefficient varies by country from −0.122 SD (Netherlands) to +0.160 SD (Israel); examples include Israel +0.160*** (SE 0.028) and Hong Kong SAR −0.079*** (SE 0.027). 2SLS (Table 2): positive influence in 18 countries (range 0.64 SD to 3.13 SD) and null influence in 16 countries; instrument weak in French-speaking Belgium, Canada, France, Ireland, and Northern Ireland per Stock & Yogo (2005).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 & 2016 Grade 4 Reading data for 39 countries, the study leveraged FSECE attendance (0-3 years) alongside student sex, student age, reading time at home, and books at home to estimate fourth-grade reading achievement, finding that attending the first stage of early childhood education has a positive influence on reading scores in 18 countries and a null influence in 16 countries (with weak-instrument concerns in several countries). This indicates that expanding access to the first stage of early childhood education may improve early reading outcomes in many contexts, but effects are heterogeneous and causal interpretation is limited by instrument strength and unobserved confounding.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes the influence of enrolment in the first stage of early childhood education (ISCED 0, ages 0–3; FSECE) on fourth-grade reading scores using PIRLS 2011 and PIRLS 2016 data for 39 overlapping countries. The outcome is students’ standardized reading achievement (mean 0, SD 1), and the authors apply PIRLS-recommended practices: student weights, jackknife repeated replication weights, and five plausible values. They first estimate an OLS model and then use a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables approach to move beyond simple correlation, using mother’s occupation as the instrument. Results show positive effects in 18 countries (2SLS effects reported as roughly 0.64 SD to 3.13 SD) and null effects in 16 countries, while the instrument is weak in French-speaking Belgium, Canada, France, Ireland, and Northern Ireland based on Stock and Yogo (2005). Limitations include potential unobservables, instrument timing mismatch (measured in fourth grade), and missing-data handling not being explicitly documented.
